wiAntiManip.title: Anti-manipulation
wiAntiManip.subtitle: How CLOB-based prediction markets can be manipulated — and how AFOS detects it
wiAntiManip.intro: This article explains, in plain language, the mechanics attackers use against prediction markets like Polymarket and describes the defenses AFOS implements to detect them. The audience is journalists, analysts, and civic-minded readers — not professional traders.
wiAntiManip.section1P1: Prediction markets like Polymarket have become a recurring source in election coverage. Major outlets cite their probabilities as a barometer of global political sentiment, commentators on X post screenshots of the prices, and Brazilian portals translate those lines as if they were opinion polls.
wiAntiManip.section1P2: The problem: these markets are not polls. They are order books — and in markets with shallow liquidity, moving the UI price costs far less than it appears. The consequence: the probability shown on screen can be fabricated by an attacker with a few tens of thousands of dollars and a short window of time.
wiAntiManip.section1P3: This page describes the mechanics, shows real numerical examples with Brazilian 2026 markets, and maps each attack pattern to the AFOS rule that tries to detect it.
wiAntiManip.section2P1: Polymarket uses a CLOB (Central Limit Order Book) — the same model as traditional exchanges. For each candidate in an election there is a binary market ("Will X win?") with two sides: YES and NO. Buyers post bids ("I'll buy YES at $0.14") and sellers post asks ("I'll sell YES at $0.15"). The market price is the midpoint between the best bid and the best ask.
wiAntiManip.section2P4: A book lists every open order at every price tick. "Depth" is how much capital sits at each level. A thick book can absorb a large order without moving the price; a thin book moves fast.
wiAntiManip.section2H2: Why thin books allow large moves with little capital
wiAntiManip.section2P5: In long-tail markets — candidates with 1% to 15% chance — books tend to be thin. There is little liquidity on either side because the outcome looks unlikely and nobody wants to tie up capital there. The result: a few thousand dollars can sweep dozens of ticks at once.
wiAntiManip.section2H3: Numerical example — Candidate X (BR Presidency 2026, illustrative)
wiAntiManip.section2ExampleP1: In a hypothetical market "Will Candidate X win the 2026 Brazilian presidential election?" (didactic only, {asOf}):
wiAntiManip.section2ExampleBullet4: A buy of roughly $13,430 in YES asks lifts the top of the book to about 30.23%
wiAntiManip.section2ExampleP2: In other words: with a little over $13k, someone can roughly double a candidate's apparent probability. The same move on Lula (YES ≈ 45.5%, deeper book) would cost much more. On Tarcísio (YES ≈ 0.35%, but $11.4M in traded volume is itself a sign of anomaly) the impact would depend on local depth.
wiAntiManip.section3Title: The NegRisk constraint — why it's not a free-for-all
wiAntiManip.section3P1: Polymarket implements the NegRisk system on multi-candidate elections. Under NegRisk a mathematical constraint holds: the sum of probabilities that each candidate wins cannot exceed 1.
wiAntiManip.section3P2: If Lula is at 45%, Tarcísio at 1%, Renan at 14%, etc., the NegRiskAdapter keeps the sum coherent via smart contracts. Artificially pushing one candidate up would, in principle, require pushing others down — and arbitrage bots exploit any mismatch between sibling markets to lock in risk-free profit.
wiAntiManip.section3P3: That is the natural defense mechanism: arbitrage-linking via the NegRiskAdapter tends to undo manipulations that violate the constraint. But — and this is the crucial point — that mechanism takes time.
wiAntiManip.section4Title: The manipulation window — arbitrage takes time
wiAntiManip.section4P1: Arbitrage bots take minutes to hours to react. They depend on:
wiAntiManip.section4Bullet1: Detecting the violation (computing Σ P across all candidates in the same event)
wiAntiManip.section4Bullet2: Having allocatable capital to take the opposite side
wiAntiManip.section4Bullet3: Posting orders in multiple markets simultaneously
wiAntiManip.section4Bullet4: Waiting for matches — which can take a while if the counterparty has also vanished
wiAntiManip.section4P2: During that interval — which can be minutes for liquid markets, or hours for long-tail markets — the price shown in the UI is the manipulated price. And that's exactly the price that gets captured in screenshots, quoted in tweets, embedded in headlines.
wiAntiManip.section4Callout: The damage from prediction-market manipulation is rarely financial. It's narrative. When a headline says "markets give X a 30% chance," that sentence circulates for days, even if the price was reverted by arbitrage within an hour.
wiAntiManip.section5P1: A sophisticated attacker rarely buys only one side. The multi-leg pattern combines:
wiAntiManip.section5Bullet1: Push: buy YES of the target candidate until the price rises to the desired level
wiAntiManip.section5Bullet2: Suppress: buy NO of rival candidates to reinforce the relative narrative
wiAntiManip.section5Bullet3: Defend: post deep bids/asks on both sides to resist arbitrage
wiAntiManip.section5P2: The cost doubles or triples versus a single-leg attack, but the duration of the manipulation grows proportionally. Arbitrage bots hesitate against attackers with "ammunition" — visible capital in the book signals that the counterparty is willing to defend the price, and the arbitrage becomes less attractive.
wiAntiManip.section5P3: This pattern is especially effective in markets with weak NegRisk (few active sub-markets) or during low-liquidity windows (UTC overnight, weekends).
wiAntiManip.section6CaseCapital: ≈ $80M in bets, ≈ $85M in net profit (figures disputed — Tsang & Yang 2026, paper [2] below, restated aggregate volume from $958M to $391M after mint/burn correction)
wiAntiManip.section6CaseMechanism: 11 proxy wallets funded from linked sources; ~1,600 trades in 24h fragmented to evade detection thresholds; concentration on Trump @ ~$0.55–0.60
wiAntiManip.section6CaseDetection: Chainalysis identified the cluster via funding clustering (common funding origin) plus trade fragmentation — a classic Sybil-with-iceberg pattern
wiAntiManip.section6CaseOutcome: Trump won the election — the operator (nicknamed "Théo") realized profit. But the informational-integrity point is different: for weeks, headlines in Bloomberg, NYT and Reuters quoted "the market gives Trump X%" without disclosing that most of that price came from 11 wallets coordinated by a single actor.
wiAntiManip.section6P1: The point is not whether the attacker "got it right" or "got it wrong." It's that even if Théo had lost the bet, the narrative attack would have paid off: for months, global public opinion consumed a unilaterally-constructed probability as if it were the aggregate signal of thousands of participants.
wiAntiManip.section7Intro: The episodes below cover direct manipulation, oracle failures, insider trading on classified information, phantom-market scams, and structural inefficiencies. Each one illuminates a distinct risk vector for prediction markets.
wiAntiManip.case2WashTradingCapital: ≈ $1 billion in suspect volume out of a $2.7B presidential market
wiAntiManip.case2WashTradingMechanism: Self-trading and round-tripping inflating reported volume; early analyses conflated share counts with USD, overstating the headline figure
wiAntiManip.case2WashTradingDetection: Chaos Labs estimated roughly one-third of the presidential market's volume was circular; Inca Digital corroborated with independent clustering
wiAntiManip.case2WashTradingOutcome: Polymarket adjusted its volume methodology (netting share mint/burn) — no regulatory enforcement followed
wiAntiManip.case3UmaOracleTitle: UMA oracle governance attack — "Ukraine mineral deal" (Mar 2025)
wiAntiManip.case3UmaOracleCapital: $7M in market open interest; attacker controlled ~5M UMA tokens
wiAntiManip.case3UmaOracleMechanism: Polymarket uses UMA's optimistic oracle for resolution; the attacker split 5M UMA across three addresses to amass ~25% of voting power and forced a "YES" resolution on a factually false claim that Ukraine had signed Trump's mineral deal (no such deal existed at the time)
wiAntiManip.case3UmaOracleDetection: On-chain analysis of UMA transfers right before the voting window combined with clustering of the voting addresses
wiAntiManip.case3UmaOracleOutcome: $7M paid out on a factually wrong resolution; Polymarket called it "unprecedented" and refused refunds, stating "this wasn't a market failure"
wiAntiManip.case4VanDykeTitle: US soldier and "Operation Absolute Resolve" — Venezuela/Maduro (Jan 2026)
wiAntiManip.case4VanDykeDate: Bets placed Dec 27, 2025 – Jan 26, 2026; military operation on Jan 3, 2026
wiAntiManip.case4VanDykeMechanism: US Army Master Sergeant Gannon Ken Van Dyke used classified knowledge of an imminent operation to capture Nicolás Maduro, buying YES on "Maduro removal" and "US intervention" markets
wiAntiManip.case4VanDykeDetection: WSJ and NPR identified a freshly-created wallet with an abnormally clean record betting on a low-prior-probability event; DOJ then indicted Van Dyke
wiAntiManip.case4VanDykeOutcome: Indictment unsealed in SDNY in April 2026; Rep. Ritchie Torres introduced H.R. 7004 ("Public Integrity in Financial Prediction Markets Act of 2026") prohibiting federal officials from trading prediction-market contracts on government policy
wiAntiManip.case4VanDykeSources: DOJ press release; NPR; Congress.gov H.R. 7004; Rep. Torres press release
wiAntiManip.case5IranPatternDate: Multiple bets between Oct 2024 and Feb 2026
wiAntiManip.case5IranPatternCapital: Five-figure wagers totaling ≈ $967k in profit at a 93% win rate on tickets ≥ $10k
wiAntiManip.case5IranPatternMechanism: Bets placed hours before unannounced Israeli strikes (Oct 2024), US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities (Jun 2025), and a joint US–Israeli surprise attack (Feb 2026)
wiAntiManip.case5IranPatternDetection: Bubblemaps' wallet-clustering analysis surfaced the pattern via funding-graph inspection
wiAntiManip.case5IranPatternOutcome: Israeli authorities indicted two individuals — including a military reservist — for allegedly using classified material to bet on Polymarket
wiAntiManip.case6AugurInvalidCapital: Specific capital not published; affected multiple ETH-price markets
wiAntiManip.case6AugurInvalidMechanism: Attacker created markets with deliberately ambiguous wording (e.g., March ETH price expiring April 1, 2024 01:59 UTC), bet against the consensus outcome, then staked REP on "invalid" resolution. When the market resolved invalid the pot was distributed equally among all participants — the attacker captured an outsized share since most weren't expecting an invalid resolution
wiAntiManip.case6AugurInvalidDetection: Community surveillance; Binance Research write-up; the validity-bond mechanism was malfunctioning
wiAntiManip.case6AugurInvalidOutcome: Augur rolled out the "Lituus" oracle and Migration-Based Universe Forking to mitigate the vector
wiAntiManip.case6AugurInvalidSources: Brave New Coin; Cointelegraph; Augur Lituus whitepaper
wiAntiManip.case7PredictItCapital: Not applicable — structural inefficiency, not a coordinated attack
wiAntiManip.case7PredictItMechanism: Markets stayed open after Biden's decisive win; the "Biden wins" contract traded below $0.95 because of contest narratives and PredictIt's withdrawal-fee structure, which made arbitrage uneconomic on small sums
wiAntiManip.case7PredictItDetection: Public write-ups (Aiden Singh) documented the prolonged inefficiency and operational friction
wiAntiManip.case7PredictItOutcome: Extended arbitrage failure — instructive about how narrative × thin liquidity × operational friction can sustain mispricing without any active manipulation
wiAntiManip.academicIntro: The empirical and theoretical literature on prediction-market manipulation has matured over the last five years. The papers below are the core references that inform AFOS's detection choices.
wiAntiManip.paper1Summary: Field experiment across 817 Manifold Markets that randomly shocked prices by 5 percentage points and tracked 600,000 hourly observations over 30 days. Headline finding: manipulated prices stayed statistically elevated even 60 days after the shock. Reversion is fast in week one and slow thereafter. Markets are less manipulable when they have more traders, higher volume, external cross-listing, and active comments. The first large-scale empirical confirmation that Hanson's theoretical robustness breaks in practice.
wiAntiManip.paper2Title: The Anatomy of a Blockchain Prediction Market
wiAntiManip.paper2Summary: Transaction-level decomposition of every Polygon trade on the Trump market. Headline numbers: naive volume aggregation overstated October Trump-market activity at $958M; share mint/burn-corrected it falls to $391M. Kyle's λ dropped from 0.53 to 0.01 over the campaign. Conclusion on Théo: bidirectional flow is inconsistent with one-sided manipulation.
wiAntiManip.paper3Title: Information Aggregation and Manipulation in an Experimental Market
wiAntiManip.paper3Citation: Hanson, Oprea & Porter (2006), Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization
wiAntiManip.paper3Summary: Foundational experiment: even when a subset of traders is paid to push prices in the wrong direction, informed traders typically arbitrage them away — conditional on enough informed traders being present. The caveat (sparse informed traders ⇒ persistent manipulation) is exactly what Rasooly & Rozzi confirm 19 years later.
wiAntiManip.paper4Title: Spoofing and Price Manipulation in Order-Driven Markets
wiAntiManip.paper4Summary: Closed-form solution for the optimal spoofer's strategy in a Kyle-style market. Relevant because spoofing — posting non-bona-fide orders cancelled before execution — is undetectable from Polymarket's on-chain settlement data alone, since cancelled orders never touch Polygon.
wiAntiManip.paper5Summary: Markets that inform a decision suffer from manipulability: an agent who benefits from a particular decision has an incentive to exaggerate the probability of a suboptimal option. Relevant to election markets that may influence campaign behavior or media narratives.
wiAntiManip.brContextIntro: Brazil's regulatory landscape changed abruptly in 2026. This section maps Anatel's block on Polymarket, the legal framework governing electoral polls, and the specific risks for the 2026 Brazilian presidential election.
wiAntiManip.brContextAnatelBody: On April 24, 2026, Finance Minister Dario Durigan announced that Anatel would block 27–28 prediction-market platforms including Polymarket and Kalshi. The block took effect within hours. Legal basis: a CMN resolution prohibiting derivatives whose underlying assets are tied to "real or virtual events of political, electoral, social, cultural or entertainment nature." Enforcement was delegated to CVM (Brazil's SEC equivalent) effective May 4, 2026.
wiAntiManip.brContextAnatelNote: ISP-level DNS blocks can be circumvented with a VPN, but Polymarket is now formally classified as illegal betting infrastructure in Brazil.
wiAntiManip.brContextTseBody: Any entity conducting an electoral poll must register it with the TSE up to 5 days before publication. Penalties: 50,000–100,000 UFIRs in fines for an unregistered poll; 6–12 months of detention for a fraudulent one.
wiAntiManip.brContextTseCrossRefBody: A Polymarket market on the Brazilian election is functionally an unregistered poll under Art. 33: it bypasses every disclosure requirement (methodology, sample, sponsor) that the law imposes.
wiAntiManip.brContextRisksTitle: Three concrete risks for Brazil in 2026
wiAntiManip.brContextRisk1: Imported price manipulation by foreign actors — a wallet with a few tens of thousands of dollars can move a candidate's apparent probability, and that probability can be quoted by Brazilian outlets.
wiAntiManip.brContextRisk2: Insider trading on unreleased polls — any actor with advance access to a registered-but-embargoed poll can trade on Polymarket before official publication.
wiAntiManip.brContextRisk3: Cross-jurisdictional enforcement gap — TSE has no mechanism to subpoena Polygon data, and CVM's jurisdiction over non-Brazilian blockchain settlement is contested.
wiAntiManip.methodologyIntro: The methods below are the tools currently used (or that could be used) to identify manipulation in prediction markets. Each covers a different vector — and together they still leave a meaningful gap.
wiAntiManip.method1Desc: Deterministic clustering from ground-truth seeds — only merges addresses with direct evidence (shared funding source, co-spending, exchange withdrawal traces). In May 2026 Polymarket formally retained Chainalysis to build a real-time insider-trading surveillance pipeline.
wiAntiManip.method2Desc: Performed the October 2024 wash-trading analyses, isolating circular volume from volume with genuine economic counterparties.
wiAntiManip.method3Desc: Clusters wallets via funding graphs; it was the tool that surfaced the Iran-strikes serial bettor by exposing the funding tree across the trader's accounts.
wiAntiManip.method4Desc: Attribution dashboards with partial Polymarket coverage — historically skewed toward whales already named in the press.
wiAntiManip.methodGapBody: SEC MIDAS and CFTC systems capture order cancellations in regulated markets. No equivalent structure exists for Polymarket: cancelled orders are never broadcast on-chain, so layering/spoofing detection would require Polymarket cooperation in handing over its off-chain order log — which is not publicly auditable. This is the single most important detection gap today.
wiAntiManip.methodAfosTitle: What AFOS can replicate without proprietary data
wiAntiManip.methodAfosBullet1: Funding-source clustering via Polygon (proxy-wallet funding transactions)
wiAntiManip.methodAfosBullet2: Behavioral co-trading clustering (wallets that enter together, on the same markets, in similar time windows)
wiAntiManip.methodAfosBullet3: Asymmetric-information event-window flagging (bets on low-prior-probability events that precede publicly unknown facts)

wiAntiManip.section8P1: AFOS runs a set of detection rules against every ingested wallet. The table below maps known attack patterns to the rules that try to catch them.
wiAntiManip.section8RowCrossPattern: Σ P violation across sibling markets
wiAntiManip.section8P2: There are still gaps. Real-time NegRisk-violation detection (the proposed cross_sibling_arb_violation rule) requires synchronized snapshots across every sub-market of an event — a pipeline that is still in design. Detection of coordinated narrative pressure (the same wallet generating the spike that becomes the headline) is another vector we intend to cover.
wiAntiManip.section9P1: AFOS is open-source and civic-tech by conviction. The code lives at github.com/AFOS-Analytics/afos-analitica-2026 and accepts contributions of any kind:
wiAntiManip.section9Bullet1: Report suspicious wallets — open an issue with address and evidence (book screenshots, timing patterns, Polygonscan transaction links)
wiAntiManip.section9Bullet2: Propose new detection rules — describe the attack pattern, the heuristic, suggested parameters
wiAntiManip.section9Bullet3: Improve the UI and the documentation — pull requests welcome in pt-BR, en and es
wiAntiManip.section9Bullet4: Validate our findings — if you are a journalist or researcher, we can share datasets under agreement
wiAntiManip.section9P2: We don't charge, we don't sell the data, we have no investors behind us. The motivation is informational: we want headlines about "what the market says" to come with proper skepticism about who is moving the market.
wiAntiManip.glossaryDef1: Central Limit Order Book — a centralized order book, the model used by traditional exchanges and by Polymarket. Buyers and sellers post limit orders, and the matching engine pairs anyone willing to transact at the same price.
wiAntiManip.glossaryDef2: Polymarket system that enforces Σ P(candidate_i) ≤ 1 across sibling markets of a single event. Guaranteed by smart contracts (NegRiskAdapter) and by arbitrage bots.
wiAntiManip.glossaryDef3: A (smart-contract) wallet that trades on Polymarket on behalf of an EOA (Externally Owned Account) controlled by the user. Each user has a distinct proxy, and identifying the owner EOA is part of AFOS's work.
wiAntiManip.glossaryDef4: Externally Owned Account — a wallet controlled by a private key (as opposed to a smart-contract). It's the entity that signs transactions and, in the Polymarket context, funds the proxy.
wiAntiManip.glossaryDef5: Attack in which a single entity controls multiple seemingly distinct identities. In the Polymarket context: many proxy wallets controlled by the same EOA or funded from the same source.
wiAntiManip.glossaryDef6: Fictitious trade in which A sells to B and B sells back to A (or similar cycle), inflating volume without changing net economic exposure. Used to simulate market interest or to qualify for incentives.
wiAntiManip.glossaryDef7: Splitting a large order into many small orders, executed over time, to hide the real intent. Confuses detection that only looks at average trade size.
wiAntiManip.glossaryDef8: The mechanism that keeps NegRisk coherent in practice: bots monitor Σ P across every sibling market and take the other side of any mismatch, restoring the constraint.
wiAntiManip.glossaryDef9: Average between the best bid and the best ask on a book. It's the probability displayed on Polymarket's UI and the typical reference for newspaper citations.
wiAntiManip.glossaryDef10: Each candidate in a multi-leg event has its own binary market ("Will X win?"). Markets for every candidate in the same event are "siblings" and share the NegRisk constraint.
wiAntiManip.footerNote: This page is educational. It does not constitute an accusation against any specific person or wallet. The numerical examples are illustrative and may vary as market liquidity evolves.
